        This Commission, the Administration, and bipartisan state leaders across the country are

working together to address one of the Nation’s most important policy issues: “[P]rotect[ing] retail

ratepayers”—i.e., everyday Americans and small businesses—from electric price increases caused

by large loads. 1 Driving this risk are “speculative transmission service requests by . . . large loads

. . . , which may lead to unjust and unreasonable increases in jurisdictional transmission rates.”2

As the Ratepayer Protection Pledge highlights, defending customers requires large loads to “pay[]

whether they use the power or not.” 3

        ComEd, with the support of this Commission and the Illinois Commerce Commission

(“ICC”), has been leading efforts to protect customers—including as a proud signatory of the

Ratepayer Protection Pledge. 4 Advancing these efforts in our system of cooperative federalism

has required a multi-jurisdictional approach to large loads. In Illinois, the ICC approved ComEd’s

large-load additions to its retail tariff (“Illinois Tariff”) with numerous customer protections, such

as requiring deposits for long-lead equipment.5 At the federal level, this Commission has

        A.      ComEd’s Retail Tariff Establishes Requirements for Large-Load Retail

continues to provide electric service to a retail customer only if all applicable requirements in these

General Terms and Conditions are met and maintained, and only if all applicable prerequisites for

service and continuing obligations in the tariff applicable to such retail customer are met and

maintained.” 15 The Illinois Tariff now in effect imposes specific requirements on “Large Demand

projected load ramp extending through the first ten (10) calendar years that the project will be in

II.     LEGAL STANDARD

        The parties agree that ComEd can cancel the TSA by showing that its cancellation is “just

and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.”63 The Commission has found it

just and reasonable to authorize the cancellation of a FERC-jurisdictional contract where the

agreement no longer serves a purpose (such as following the cancellation of the underlying

project), 64 or where the counterparty fails to cure a breach of its contractual obligations during the

interconnection process. 65 The Commission also considers as part of its just and reasonable

analysis harms to other market participants and to the public interest that would result from

continuing to enforce the contract following breach. 66

III.    ANSWER

        A.       Because the Retail Application Has Been Terminated by Operation of
                 ComEd’s State Tariff, It Is Just and Reasonable To Cancel the TSA.

        Because ComEd has “terminat[ed] the [Retail Application]” 67 pursuant to the Illinois

Tariff, cancellation of the TSA is just and reasonable as well. Hillwood’s TSA is expressly

premised on an active Retail Application and unambiguously conditions its effectiveness on an

active Retail Application. The TSA expressly incorporates its recitals “into the terms and

conditions,” 68 and specifies that its “purpose” is to support Hillwood “tak[ing] retail electric

delivery services” from ComEd. 69 The recitals add that ComEd “intends to service [Hillwood’s]

anticipated load pursuant to the applicable rate schedule in [ComEd’s] Retail Service Tariff.”70

The TSA further emphasizes that ComEd will proceed consistent with “its retail service

obligations[] and applicable Retail Service Tariffs.”71 ComEd’s TSA Transmittal Letter likewise

noted that the TSA’s purpose is to support ComEd’s intent “to provide . . . retail electric delivery

services.” 72

        Everything in the TSA is thus premised on the assumption that there is a project taking

retail service, and absent such a project, the TSA serves no purpose. Here, there is no such

project—because the Retail Application has been terminated. As required by its Illinois Tariff,

ComEd notified Hillwood on July 24, 2026 that based on Hillwood’s noncompliance with its Retail

Application obligations, “ComEd is terminating the [Retail Application].” 73 ComEd’s letter was

        3.      I am currently employed as a Senior Manager, T&S New Business, of

Commonwealth Edison Company (“ComEd”). I have been employed in this position since 2026.

In my role as Senior Manager, T&S New Business, I oversee the planning and execution of major

        4.      ComEd is a public utility in Illinois providing electric service in northern Illinois.

to retail customers in Illinois is governed by ComEd’s electric retail service tariff (“Tariff”) on file

with the Illinois Commerce Commission (“ICC”) that defines the rates, terms and conditions of

ComEd’s electric retail service.

        Application Process
        Below is the process to receive any type of electric service from Com Ed:


        1. Establish or Verify Your Account
          If you have an existing Com Ed account, please enter the number in the "Existing Com Ed Account#" field . If this is a new service

          customer service representative will have to contact you before your application can be processed.

        2. Complete and Submit Service Application
          Please work with a licensed electrical professional to complete your application. You have two options for submitting your
          information:
          Preferred Method: Enter your information directly into the New Business Portal on line form. You will immediately receive a
          confirmation number for tracking your project status.
          Alternative Method: You may email your completed pdf application to SeNiceApplications@ComEd.com.

        3. ComEd Representative Assigned
          A Com Ed representative will be assigned to your project, will schedule a site visit and will manage your project through
          completion .

        4. Site Visit
          Your Com Ed representative will meet you at the project site to determine how to best provide the requested service.

        5. Service Request Documentation
          After the site visit, your Com Ed representative will create all necessary contracts; provide a summary of charges, if applicable, and,
          if needed, diagrams depicting the service.

        6. Service Authorization
          Review all documents provided by your Com Ed representative, sign and return them to your representative along with payment, if
          applicable, to authorize work to begin.

        7. "Service Need" Date Determination
          The "start work" and "service need" dates will be negotiated with you and every effort will be made to meet your "preferred
          service" date. Delays in submitting the necessary documentation or changes to the project may adversely impact the "service
          need" date.

        8. "Service Need" Date Confirmation
          Four weeks prior to the "start work" date, your Com Ed representative will contact you to confirm whether work can begin. If the
          work cannot begin, the "start work" and "service need" dates will be adjusted accordingly. The new dates will be subject to Com Ed's
          workload and resource availability.

        9. Final Inspection
          Two weeks prior to the "start work" date, Com Ed will perform an on-site inspection to verify the site is ready for work to begin. If the
          site is not ready, Com Ed will let you know what needs to be done to make the site ready. Com Ed reserves the right to reschedule
          the "start work" and "service need" dates based on the work required to make the site ready.
